analogy.p: Imagine the temperature is the water level and the energy supplied is water poured in. A material with a **high specific heat capacity** is like a very wide bucket: you pour in a lot of water (energy) and the level (temperature) rises only a little. A low-c metal is a thin tube: the same amount poured in makes the level shoot up. The mass is like having several buckets side by side, so more mass needs more water for the same rise. The analogy breaks down because a bucket does not leak through the sides in a way that matches heat loss to surroundings, whereas real blocks lose more energy the hotter they get.

bullets: Symbol: **c**. Unit: **joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg°C**.
Water has a very high specific heat capacity, **4200 J/kg°C**: it takes 4200 J to warm 1 kg of water by 1°C.
Metals have much lower values (for example aluminium is roughly 900 J/kg°C and copper roughly 385 J/kg°C), so they heat up and cool down much faster than water for the same energy transfer.
**High c** = a lot of energy needed for each degree = the material heats and cools **slowly**. **Low c** = little energy needed per degree = heats and cools **quickly**.
A temperature change of 1°C is the same size as a change of 1 K, which is why you may also see J/kg K, but AQA papers use J/kg°C.
Specific heat capacity is about **temperature change within one state**; it is different from specific latent heat (4.3), which is about energy to change state with no temperature change.
core.p: When you heat an object, energy is transferred to its **thermal energy store** and its temperature rises. But the same amount of energy does not raise every material's temperature by the same amount. The **specific heat capacity** of a substance is **the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius**. It is a property of the material, not of the object, so a teaspoon of water and a swimming pool of water have exactly the same specific heat capacity. It matters because it tells you how much energy you must supply (or how much will be released) when the temperature of a known mass of a known material changes.

bullets: **ΔE** = change in thermal energy, in **joules (J)**.
**m** = mass, in **kilograms (kg)**. Convert grams by dividing by 1000 (500 g = 0.500 kg).
**c** = specific heat capacity, in **J/kg°C**.
**Δθ** = temperature change, in **°C**, and is **final temperature minus initial temperature**.
If the temperature rises, Δθ is positive and energy is gained; if it falls, energy is released to the surroundings.
The equation only works while the substance stays in the same state (no melting or boiling during the change).
Doubling the mass, or doubling the temperature change, doubles the energy needed: ΔE is **directly proportional** to both m and Δθ.
core.h: The equation: change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change
core.p: You must be able to **recall and apply** this equation. It is **change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change**, written **ΔE = m c Δθ**. It follows directly from the definition: if 1 kg needs c joules for each degree, then m kilograms need m x c joules for each degree, and Δθ degrees need m x c x Δθ joules. Always check that the mass is in kilograms before substituting.

bullets: To find mass: **m = ΔE / (c Δθ)**.
To find specific heat capacity: **c = ΔE / (m Δθ)**. This is the form used in the required practical.
To find temperature change: **Δθ = ΔE / (m c)**, then add it to the starting temperature for the final temperature.
Unit check: J = kg x J/kg°C x °C. The kg cancel and the °C cancel, leaving J, so the units are consistent.
Common slip: using Δθ as the **final** temperature instead of the **change**. Always subtract.
Give answers to a sensible number of significant figures (usually the same as the least precise data value) and always include the unit.
core.h: Rearranging the equation and checking units
core.p: Exam questions rarely ask for ΔE every time, so you need to rearrange confidently. Treat the equation as a product of three terms and divide by the two you know. Writing the rearrangement as a separate line before substituting earns the method mark even if the arithmetic slips. Always finish with a quick sense check: water needs lots of energy, metals need little.

bullets: The temperature of a substance is linked to the **average kinetic energy** of its particles; to raise the temperature the particles must gain kinetic energy.
Not all supplied energy goes into kinetic energy, so materials with a high c 'soak up' more energy per degree.
Because the same energy raises a low-c metal's temperature by more, metals feel hot quickly in sunshine while water in a lake warms slowly.
The values for different materials are found **experimentally**, which is what the required practical does.
Specific heat capacity is given in the question for most materials, but **4200 J/kg°C for water** is commonly quoted and worth remembering.
core.h: Why different materials have different specific heat capacities
core.p: When energy is transferred to a material, it is shared between the **kinetic energy stores** of the particles (making them vibrate or move faster, which is what raises the temperature) and the **potential energy stores** associated with the forces between the particles. Different materials store the energy in different ways, so some need much more energy than others for each degree of temperature rise. Water, with strong forces between its molecules and many ways of storing energy, has an unusually high value. You are not required to explain the particle detail in depth, but it helps you understand why c is a measured property of each material.

bullets: **Energy transferred = power x time, E = P t** (E in J, P in W, t in s).
For an electrical heater, **P = V I** (potential difference x current), so **E = V I t**.
A **joulemeter** can display the energy transferred directly, which saves calculating.
Example: a 50 W heater on for 4 minutes: t = 240 s, E = 50 x 240 = **12 000 J**.
Convert minutes to seconds every time: this is one of the most common lost marks.
If you use a 12 V supply and measure 4.2 A, P = 12 x 4.2 = 50.4 W, so the 'power rating' and measured power can differ slightly.
core.h: Where the energy comes from: electrical heating
core.p: In the required practical the energy comes from an **electric heater**, so the energy transferred electrically to the heater must be calculated or measured. The heater transfers energy to the thermal energy store of the material. The energy supplied depends on the **power** of the heater and the **time** it is on. This links 4.1 (Energy) to 4.2 (Electricity), and you should be able to move between the equations quickly.

bullets: **Apparatus:** a block of known material (about 1 kg), an electric immersion heater (for example 50 W, 12 V), a low-voltage power supply (or a joulemeter), an ammeter and voltmeter if no joulemeter, a thermometer (or temperature probe), a **top-pan balance**, a stopwatch, **insulation** (such as a thick layer of cotton wool or a lagged jacket) and a little oil.
A **few drops of oil** in the thermometer hole (and heater hole) improve **thermal contact** between the thermometer and the block, so the reading is accurate.
The **independent variable** is the energy supplied (changed by running the heater for longer); the **dependent variable** is the temperature of the block.
**Control variables:** mass of the block, the material, the heater power, and the insulation.

The same method works for liquids such as water: use a **lagged beaker or polystyrene cup**, an immersion heater and a **stirrer**, and calculate the mass of liquid from a balance (subtract the beaker mass).
core.h: Required practical: aim and apparatus (solid block)
core.p: The aim is to **investigate the specific heat capacity of one or more materials**, linking the decrease in one energy store (the electrical energy supplied) to the increase in the thermal energy store and the temperature rise of the material. The most common version uses a solid block, usually of aluminium, copper or steel, of known mass with two holes drilled in it: one for an electric immersion heater and one for a thermometer. Everything is wrapped in insulation to reduce energy transfer to the surroundings.

bullets: **1.** Measure the **mass of the block** with a balance and record it in kg.
**2.** Fit the heater and thermometer in the holes, adding a little oil for good thermal contact, then wrap the block in insulation.
**3.** Record the **initial temperature** of the block.
**4.** Connect the heater to the power supply (with ammeter and voltmeter, or a joulemeter) and switch on, starting the stopwatch at the same time.
**5.** Record the **potential difference and current** (or joulemeter reading) so the power can be calculated, and note the time.
**6.** Take **temperature readings at regular intervals**, for example every minute for about 10 minutes.
**7.** Switch off the heater and keep watching the thermometer: the temperature often keeps **rising for a short while**, so record the **highest temperature** reached.
**8.** Calculate the energy supplied using **E = V I t** (or read it from the joulemeter) and the temperature rise Δθ.
**9.** Calculate **c = ΔE / (m Δθ)**, then repeat and find a mean.
core.h: Required practical: method step by step
core.p: Follow a clear sequence and say why each step is done; examiners reward methods that are reproducible and sensibly ordered. The key physics is that the electrical energy supplied is assumed to end up as thermal energy in the block, so the temperature rise gives you c.

bullets: Plot **energy supplied (J)** on the x-axis (calculate E = P t for each time) and **temperature (°C)** on the y-axis; use a ruler and a line of best fit.
**Gradient = Δθ / ΔE = 1 / (m c)**, therefore **c = 1 / (m x gradient)**.
Worked idea: if the gradient is 0.0022 °C/J for a 0.50 kg block, c = 1 / (0.50 x 0.0022) = about 910 J/kg°C.
A line that **curves and flattens** at higher temperatures shows increasing energy loss to the surroundings, because the hotter the block, the faster it loses energy.
A **straight line through the origin** (when plotting temperature **rise**) shows direct proportionality between energy supplied and temperature rise.
Identify any **anomalous** point (well off the trend), and say whether you would ignore it in the mean.
Compare your value with the data-book value: a result that is too high or low is usually explained by energy losses rather than a mistake in the physics.
core.h: Processing results and using a graph
core.p: With readings taken at intervals you can plot a graph rather than rely on one pair of numbers, which makes the result more reliable. Because ΔE = m c Δθ, the temperature rise is directly proportional to the energy supplied, so a graph of **temperature (y) against energy supplied (x)** should be a straight line through the starting temperature. The gradient of that line is **Δθ / ΔE = 1 / (m c)**, so you can find c from it. Using a line of best fit averages out random errors and highlights anomalies.

bullets: While the heater is on, a straight section means energy is transferred to the block at a steady rate (constant power).
The gradient of temperature against time is steeper for a smaller mass or a smaller c, with the same heater power.
After switch-off the reading can rise a little further: always record the **maximum** temperature, not the value at switch-off.
Temperature change = maximum temperature - initial temperature.
A line that flattens while the heater is still on shows increasing energy loss to the surroundings.
The slow fall after the peak shows the block cooling by conduction, convection and radiation to the surroundings.
To convert to energy supplied use E = P t at each time (time in seconds).
core.h: Reading a temperature-time graph and the overshoot
core.p: If you record the temperature at regular times while the heater is on, the graph of temperature against time rises steadily, and its gradient depends on the heater power, the mass and the specific heat capacity. When the heater is switched off the thermometer often keeps rising for a short while, because energy stored in the hot heater element and the metal near it is still spreading through the block, and the thermometer bulb takes time to respond. The highest reading is therefore the best estimate of the final temperature, and the temperature rise is the maximum minus the starting value. After the peak the temperature falls slowly because the block loses energy to its surroundings.

bullets: **Energy loss to the surroundings** by conduction, convection and radiation: improve with **better insulation** (thicker lagging, a lid, or insulating the top and base too).
The thermometer reading may lag behind the true temperature: use **oil** for contact and **wait for the maximum** reading after switching off.
The heater also warms the insulation and apparatus, so not all the energy goes into the block.
The thermometer has a limited resolution (for example 1°C), giving a large percentage error on small rises: **use a larger temperature change**, or a digital probe with finer resolution.
Reading the thermometer from the wrong angle causes **parallax error**: read at eye level.
A **joulemeter** removes errors in calculating energy from V, I and t.
**Repeat the experiment** and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of random error, and compare against the known value to judge accuracy.
core.h: Sources of error and how to improve accuracy
core.p: The biggest source of error is **energy transferred to the surroundings** rather than into the thermal energy store of the block. Because the calculation assumes all the supplied energy heats the block, the actual temperature rise is smaller than predicted, so Δθ is too small and the calculated **c is too large**. Other errors come from poor thermal contact, thermometer lag and time-keeping. Examiners want you to name the problem, say its effect, and give a specific improvement.

bullets: **Hot heater and block** can cause burns: allow to cool before handling, keep the heater switched off when moving anything, and run burns under cold water for at least five minutes.
**Electrical hazard:** keep water and wires away from each other, check cables are not frayed, and never switch on the heater when it is out of the liquid or block.
For liquids, the immersion heater should be **fully covered** by the liquid, otherwise it can overheat and crack the beaker.
Take care with hot water spills: use a stable surface and do not overfill the beaker.
A heavy block can be dropped: lift carefully and keep feet clear.
Tie back long hair and keep bags off the floor; wear eye protection if there is any chance of splashing hot water.
core.h: Risks and safety in the required practical
core.p: Risk assessments are often examined as short-answer questions. State the **hazard** (what could cause harm), the **risk** (what could happen) and a sensible **control measure**. In this practical the main hazards are hot equipment and electricity near liquids.

bullets: Independent: **energy supplied** (or time the heater is on at fixed power).
Dependent: **temperature of the material**.
Control: **mass**, **material**, **heater power**, **insulation**, and the starting temperature.
If you compare materials, use the **same mass and same energy** so you can compare the temperature rises directly.
Repeat and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability.
Using a more precise thermometer and a joulemeter improves **accuracy and resolution** but does not change what is measured.
core.p: Being able to describe variables precisely is a standard skill in all required practicals. The **independent variable** is what you change, the **dependent variable** is what you measure, and **control variables** are kept the same so the test is fair (valid). The investigation is valid when only the independent variable affects the dependent variable, and reliable when repeating gives similar results.

bullets: Rise in temperature = energy / (m c); same energy and mass means the **bigger c gives the smaller rise**.
Water: 1000 / (1 x 4200) = 0.24 degrees C; aluminium: 1000 / (1 x 900) = 1.1 degrees C; copper: 1000 / (1 x 385) = 2.6 degrees C.
To compare fairly, use the same mass, the same energy (same power and time) and the same starting temperature.
A material with a high c is a good **store of energy** (water in central heating); a low c suits cooking pans that heat quickly.
The sea warms and cools more slowly than land, which makes coastal climates milder.
Values of c are given in the data in most questions, but 4200 J/kg degrees C for water is worth remembering.
core.h: Comparing materials: same energy, different temperature rise
core.p: Because the temperature change is given by change in temperature = energy / (mass x c), the same energy given to the same mass produces a smaller temperature rise in a material with a larger c. This is why you can rank materials by specific heat capacity simply by comparing their temperature rises under identical conditions. For example, putting 1000 J into 1 kg of each material gives a rise of about 0.24 degrees C for water, 1.1 degrees C for aluminium and 2.6 degrees C for copper, using approximate c values of 4200, 900 and 385 J/kg degrees C. Examiners often ask you to explain such a comparison in words, so link the energy, the mass and the c value in your sentence.

bullets: **Link to power (4.1):** time to heat = ΔE / P. Example: heating 1.5 kg of water from 20°C to 100°C needs 1.5 x 4200 x 80 = **504 000 J**; with a 2000 W kettle this takes 504 000 / 2000 = **252 s** (about 4 minutes, in an ideal case).
**Link to conservation of energy:** the energy supplied by the heater equals the energy transferred to the block plus the energy wasted to the surroundings.
**Link to efficiency:** useful energy ÷ total energy; the energy lost in this practical is the 'wasted' part.
**Link to electricity (4.2):** E = V I t and P = V I.
**Link to particle model (4.3):** specific latent heat covers changes of state, where energy is transferred but temperature stays constant.
**Higher tier extension:** you may need to combine this with equations such as E = P t, or to compare two materials given a table of c values.
core.h: Applications and links to other topics
core.p: Specific heat capacity explains many everyday and engineering situations. Water's high value makes it ideal for **central heating systems and cooling systems**, because it carries a large amount of energy for a small temperature change. Metals with low c are used for cooking pans because they heat up quickly. Seaside places have milder climates than inland areas because the sea warms and cools more slowly than land. The idea also links directly to energy conservation, power and efficiency.

exam: **State/define (1–2 marks):** specific heat capacity = energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1°C. Learn this wording exactly.
**Calculation (2–3 marks):** write the equation, rearrange, substitute with correct units (kg, °C), then give the answer with unit. Marks are for method even if the final answer is wrong.
**'Show that' questions:** show the unrounded value, then the rounded value, to prove the result.
**Convert units** (g to kg, minutes to seconds, kW to W) before substituting, and show the conversion.

**Required practical, method (4–6 marks):** mention mass of block, heater and thermometer in holes, oil, insulation, initial temperature, timing, readings at intervals, maximum temperature, and how c is calculated.

**Explain why the calculated value is higher than the true value:** energy lost to surroundings, so the temperature rise is lower than if all the energy stayed in the block, so c = E/(mΔθ) is too large.
**Suggest an improvement:** name a specific change (more insulation, a lid, a joulemeter) and say why it helps.
**Graph questions:** the gradient of temperature against energy is 1/(m c); say that a curve flattening means increasing energy loss.
**Risk assessment:** hazard, risk, control: hot heater/burns/let cool; electricity near water/dry hands, check wires.
**Comparing materials:** same mass and energy; the material with the lower c has the greater temperature rise.
**Use command words:** 'describe' means give features, 'explain' means give a reason (use 'because'), 'evaluate' means give both strengths and weaknesses, then a judgement.
**Compare two materials (2-3 marks)**: for the same mass and energy the material with the lower c has the greater temperature rise; quote delta theta = E / (m c).

mistakes.r: Convert to kilograms first: 500 g = 0.500 kg. The unit of c involves kg.
mistakes.w: Using the mass in grams (for example 500) in ΔE = m c Δθ.
Using the final temperature as Δθ.

mistakes.r: Time must be in seconds: 4 minutes = 240 s.
mistakes.w: Using minutes in E = P t.

mistakes.r: It is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1°C.
mistakes.w: Saying specific heat capacity is 'how hot something gets' or 'how much heat it holds'.

mistakes.r: Energy lost means the temperature rise is smaller than expected, so the calculated c is too large.
mistakes.w: Saying heat loss makes the calculated c too small.

mistakes.r: Keep reading and record the maximum temperature, because the temperature continues to rise briefly.
mistakes.w: Stopping the thermometer reading the moment the heater is switched off.

mistakes.r: Insulation reduces energy transfer to the surroundings, so more of the supplied energy increases the block's thermal energy store.
mistakes.w: Saying insulation 'keeps the cold out' or 'traps heat' without detail.

mistakes.r: Oil improves thermal contact between the thermometer and the block so the reading is more accurate.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the oil in the thermometer hole or giving no reason for it.
Leaving out the unit or giving J/kg only.

mistakes.r: A high c needs a lot of energy per degree, so the material heats up and cools down slowly.
mistakes.w: Saying a material with a high specific heat capacity heats up quickly.

summary: You must recall and use ΔE = m c Δθ, define specific heat capacity as the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C, and describe and evaluate the required practical that finds c by electrically heating a known mass of material. It matters because it links energy, temperature and power, and it is a guaranteed practical-skills topic in Paper 1.

terms.d: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.
The energy store associated with the kinetic and potential energy of the particles in an object; it increases when an object is heated.
The change in thermal energy, measured in joules (J).
The temperature change, final temperature minus initial temperature, in °C.
The unit of energy; 1 J is the energy transferred when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m.
The rate at which energy is transferred, in watts; P = E / t.
Material that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating to the surroundings.
Good transfer of energy between two touching objects, improved by using oil in the thermometer hole.
The variable you deliberately change in an investigation (energy supplied).
The variable you measure to see the effect of the change (temperature).
A variable kept the same so that the investigation is a fair test.
The slope of a line on a graph, found as change in y divided by change in x.
An instrument that measures directly the energy transferred electrically, in joules.
A result that does not fit the pattern and is well outside the expected range.
A reading error caused by viewing a scale from the wrong angle.
The smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect, such as 1 degree C on a thermometer.
Insulating material wrapped around an object or container to reduce energy transfer to the surroundings.
The highest reading reached, which continues briefly after the heater is switched off; used to find the temperature change.

worked.ans: c = 900 J/kg°C. (Real value may be slightly lower because the experiment transfers some energy to the surroundings.)
worked.q: A 0.50 kg aluminium block is heated by a 60 W heater for 5.0 minutes. The temperature rises by 40°C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium. (4 marks)
steps: Energy supplied: E = P t = 60 x 300 = 18 000 J.

worked.ans: Energy = 504 000 J (504 kJ); time = 252 s (about 4.2 minutes).
worked.q: A kettle contains 1.5 kg of water at 20°C. Calculate the energy needed to heat it to 100°C, and the time this takes in a 2000 W kettle with no energy losses. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg°C. (5 marks)
steps: Rearrange E = P t: t = E / P.

worked.ans: Some of the energy supplied by the heater is transferred to the surroundings and not to the block, so the temperature rise is smaller than it should be. Since c = E / (m Δθ), a smaller Δθ gives a larger calculated c. The student could improve this by adding more insulation (or a lid) round the block to reduce energy loss.
worked.q: A student measures c for a metal block and gets a value much higher than the data-book value. Explain why, and suggest one improvement. (3 marks)
steps: Link the error to energy transfer.
Explain the effect on Δθ and c.
